clinicalPearls: The pleural space normally holds only a thin film of fluid acting as a coupling system, kept at roughly -3 to -5 cmH2O by the balance between lung elastic recoil (visceral pleura) and chest-wall outward expansion (parietal pleura).

The first diagnostic step in any pleural effusion is distinguishing transudate from exudate via thoracentesis; this dictates whether further work-up is needed, since exudates require investigation to define their cause.

Light's criteria define an exudate when at least one is met: pleural fluid/serum protein >0.5, pleural fluid/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper normal serum limit; transudates meet none.

Light's criteria misclassify about 25% of transudates as exudates ('pseudoexudates'), often in a diuresed transudate; a serum-to-pleural-fluid protein gradient >3.1 g/dL or albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL helps reclassify these (high sensitivity in heart failure and hepatothorax).
Left ventricular failure is the single most common cause of pleural effusion (a transudate from raised hydrostatic pressure); cirrhosis is the next leading transudative cause in the United States.

Parapneumonic effusions occur in up to 50% of community-acquired pneumonias and are generally the most common exudative effusion in the U.S.; about 10% become complicated or progress to empyema (fibrinopurulent or grossly purulent fluid).

Malignant pleural effusions are the second most common exudate; lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, and lymphoma together cause roughly 75% of cases, and dyspnea is often out of proportion to effusion size.
Pulmonary embolism is the diagnosis most commonly overlooked in an undiagnosed exudative effusion; the fluid is almost always exudative and dyspnea is the predominant symptom.

Tuberculous pleuritis arises largely as a hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculous protein in the pleural space and yields a lymphocyte-predominant exudate; pleural biopsy culture yield exceeds that of pleural fluid.

Chylothorax produces milky fluid with a triglyceride level exceeding 110 mg/dL (1.2 mmol/L); prolonged chest-tube drainage should be avoided because chyle loss causes malnutrition and immunologic incompetence.
Hemothorax is defined when pleural fluid hematocrit exceeds half the peripheral blood hematocrit; most are traumatic.
About half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax (from rupture of apical subpleural blebs) will have a recurrence.
Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency: positive intrapleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle impairs ventilation and reduces venous return, lowering cardiac output.
harrison.pathophysiology: Pleural fluid normally enters from parietal pleural capillaries and is cleared by parietal pleural lymphatics, which can absorb up to 20 times the normal rate of fluid formation; fluid can also enter from lung interstitium via the visceral pleura or from the peritoneal cavity through diaphragmatic openings. An effusion forms when the hydrostatic-oncotic balance is disturbed and fluid production overwhelms lymphatic removal. Transudates result from altered systemic factors (e.g., elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure in heart failure raising hydrostatic pressure, or low oncotic pressure), whereas exudates result from altered local factors such as inflammation, infection, or malignancy increasing capillary permeability or impairing lymphatic drainage. Parapneumonic effusions begin as a sterile reactive exudate and can progress through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases. Hepatic hydrothorax reflects direct movement of ascitic fluid through small diaphragmatic defects into the pleural space. Pneumothorax results from gas entering the pleural space, abolishing the negative pressure that couples lung to chest wall; in tension pneumothorax a one-way mechanism produces sustained positive pleural pressure.
additionalDifferentials: Transudates: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal dialysis, superior vena cava obstruction, myxedema, urinothorax
Exudates from neoplasm: metastatic disease, mesothelioma, lymphoma
Exudates from infection: bacterial (parapneumonic/empyema), tuberculous, fungal, viral, parasitic
Gastrointestinal causes: esophageal perforation, pancreatic disease, intraabdominal abscess, diaphragmatic hernia, post-abdominal surgery, post liver transplant, variceal sclerotherapy
Collagen vascular disease: rheumatoid pleuritis, SLE, drug-induced lupus, Sjogren syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss

Other: post-CABG, asbestos exposure, sarcoidosis, uremia, Meigs' syndrome, yellow nail syndrome, trapped lung, radiation, post-cardiac injury syndrome, hemothorax, chylothorax, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, pericardial disease, drug-induced (nitrofurantoin, dantrolene, methysergide, bromocriptine, procarbazine, amiodarone, dasatinib)
infectionMimics: Tuberculous pleuritis presenting with fever, weight loss, and pleuritic pain mimicking malignancy or other chronic exudate
Intraabdominal abscess producing a febrile, polymorphonuclear effusion without pulmonary parenchymal abnormality
Hepatic hydrothorax that can be complicated by spontaneous bacterial empyema
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary embolism mimicking infectious pleuritis with an exudative effusion and pleuritic pain
Malignant effusion (including mesothelioma) mimicking empyema or chronic infection
Rheumatoid or lupus pleuritis mimicking infectious exudate (low glucose in rheumatoid disease)
Pleural effusion ex vacuo / trapped lung mimicking persistent active disease
additionalInvestigations: Chest imaging: chest x-ray with lateral decubitus films, chest ultrasound, and CT to assess extent, free-flowing versus loculated fluid, and to guide sampling/drainage
Diagnostic thoracentesis with pleural fluid protein and LDH (Light's criteria)
Pleural fluid glucose, differential cell count, Gram stain/culture, and cytology

Disease-specific pleural fluid tests: amylase (pancreatic disease/esophageal rupture), eosinophils (drug-induced), NT-proBNP (heart failure, >1500 pg/mL suggests cardiac origin), cholesterol/triglycerides (chylothorax, triglyceride >110 mg/dL), hematocrit (hemothorax), glucose and pH (rheumatoid disease), Congo red staining (amyloidosis), flow cytometry (lymphoma)
TB markers: pleural fluid adenosine deaminase >40 IU/L or interferon-gamma >140 pg/mL; AFB culture, pleural biopsy
CT/ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy when cytology is non-diagnostic
CT angiography for suspected pulmonary embolism; lymphangiogram and chest CT for chylothorax without obvious trauma
Pleural manometry to help confirm trapped lung
redFlags: Tension pneumothorax: enlarged hemithorax with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, contralateral mediastinal shift, and hypotension; treat as an emergency with immediate needle decompression (large-bore needle in the second anterior intercostal space).
Difficulty ventilating or high peak inspiratory pressures during mechanical ventilation/resuscitation strongly suggest tension pneumothorax.

Complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema markers indicating need for drainage: loculated fluid, pleural fluid pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL (<3.3 mmol/L), positive Gram stain or culture, gross pus, and elevated pleural fluid LDH (>900 IU/L).
Hemothorax with ongoing pleural hemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/h warrants angiographic embolization, thoracoscopy, or thoracotomy.
Secondary pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease can be more life-threatening because of reduced pulmonary reserve.
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Transudative effusions from heart failure or cirrhosis improve when the primary condition is treated, and undiagnosed viral effusions usually resolve spontaneously without long-term residua. A malignant pleural effusion usually portends a poor prognosis (often less than 6-month survival) and reflects disseminated disease that is generally not curable with chemotherapy. Untreated complicated parapneumonic effusions can organize into a restrictive pleural peel (trapped lung). Tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or marked hypoxemia if not relieved. Surgical pleurodesis prevents pneumothorax recurrence in nearly 100% of cases.
pitfalls: Relying on Light's criteria alone can misclassify roughly 25% of transudates as exudates; failing to apply protein/albumin gradients in a clinically transudative setting leads to unnecessary work-up.
Overlooking pulmonary embolism as the cause of an otherwise undiagnosed exudative effusion.
Being overly aggressive in pursuing a diagnosis in a clinically improving patient whose effusion is likely viral and self-limited.

Failing to recognize trapped lung: a thick pleural rind, air on imaging after thoracentesis (pneumothorax ex vacuo), and rapid re-accumulation indicate a lung that will not re-expand without decortication.
Prolonged tube thoracostomy drainage of a chylothorax, which can cause malnutrition and immunologic incompetence.
Not performing diagnostic thoracentesis in a presumed heart-failure effusion that is unilateral, asymmetric, febrile, or pleuritic, or that persists despite therapy.
harrison.severityClassification: Parapneumonic effusions are staged along a continuum from simple (free-flowing, reactive) to complicated (loculated, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, positive Gram stain/culture) to empyema (frank pus), with progression through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases guiding the need for escalating intervention. Pneumothorax is categorized as primary spontaneous, secondary, traumatic (including iatrogenic), and tension.
